topics.title: Malignant Spinal Cord Compression
topics.subtitle: Back pain, weakness, sensory loss, urinary retention, cancer history

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
Immediately start dexamethasone 10mg IV: do NOT delay for imaging
Get emergent MRI of entire spine (whole spine: multifocal in 10-38%)
Consult radiation oncology STAT for emergent radiothetherapy

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Known cancer dx & type (breast, lung, prostate, renal, thyroid most common)
Back pain Hx.: 90% present with back pain, worse when supine (unlike degenerative pain)
Motor weakness (75%), sensory changes, bowel/bladder dysfunction
Ambulatory status before onset: strongest predictor of outcome
Prior spinal radiation or surgery
Current oncologic tx regimen
Hx. of DVT/PE

sections.title: Exam
items: Point tenderness over spine at level of compression
Motor exam: grade strength in all extremities, note level
Sensory level: pinprick & light touch: identify dermatomal level
Rectal exam: ↓ rectal tone = cauda equina involvement
Reflexes: upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski) above conus; lower motor neuron signs (areflexia) in cauda equina
Gait assessment if safe: ambulatory status is key prognostic factor
Bladder scan for post void residual (>200mL suggests retention)

pairs.value: Compression of spinal cord or cauda equina by direct tumor extension or vertebral body collapse in setting of metastatic or primary spinal malignancy
5-10% of cancer pts; most common in breast, lung, prostate, renal cell, & thyroid cancers
Thoracic spine 70%, lumbosacral 20%, cervical 10%
Neurological outcome depends on pretx function: once paraplegia is established, recovery is rare
MCC: tumor extends from vertebral body into epidural space
Vertebral body collapse compresses cord: lytic lesions from myeloma, breast, lung, renal, thyroid
Paraspinal tumors (lymphoma, neuroblastoma) growing through neural foramen
Fever, elevated WBC/ESR, IV drug use Hx.
Anticoagulation, recent procedure
Inflammatory, MRI shows cord signal without epidural mass
Mechanical back pain, radiculopathy distribution

sections.title: Management
items: Immediate stabilization: keep spinal precautions, continue dexamethasone 4mg IV/PO q6h after the 10mg IV load, & treat pain without delaying serial neuro exams

Definitive planning: get MRI whole spine & call radiation oncology plus neurosurgery / spine surgery now. Surgery is favored for instability, singlelevel disease, retropulsed bone, radioresistant tumor, or worsening deficits; otherwise move quickly to radiation
Supportive care: Foley if retention, keep NPO if surgery possible, give DVT prophylaxis if safe, & document serial motor / sensory / bowel bladder exams
Continue dexamethasone 4mg IV/PO q6h: begin taper after radiation starts
Radiothetherapy:30 Gy in 10 fractions or 20 Gy in 5 fractions
Surgery (decompressive laminectomy ± stabilization) if: single level compression, radioresistant tumor, spinal instability, neurological deterioration during radiation
Maintain DVT prophylaxis throughout hospitalization
Physical therapy & rehabilitation consultation
Monitor neurological exam q4-6h during acute phase
GI prophylaxis (PPI) while on high dose steroids
Glucose monitoring q6h: steroidinduced hyperglycemia common

pairs.value: Gold standard: identifies level, extent, & multifocal disease (10-38%)
Alternative if MRI contraindicated (pacemaker, etc.)
Baseline labs, check renal function for contrast
Elevated in infection: helps differentiate epidural abscess
check for urinary retention
Low sensitivity (~60%): do NOT use to r/o MSCC

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.notes: Give now if MSCC suspected: before imaging. ↓ vasogenic edema. Taper over 2 weeks after definitive tx.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone (high dose)
drugs.dose: 96mg IV bolus, then 24mg IV q6h x 3 days
drugs.notes: Consider for progressive deficits or nearcomplete block on MRI. Higher complication rate.

drugs.name: Enoxaparin
drugs.notes: DVT prophylaxis: immobilized oncology pts are extremely risk for VTE.

pairs.key: ICU / immediate higher level of care if
pairs.value: persistent respiratory distress, high-flow or NIV need, hemodynamic instability, vasopressor need, severe arrhythmia, airway risk, neurologic decline, or a trajectory suggesting pt may crash on the floor.

topics.title: SVC Syndrome
topics.subtitle: Facial swelling, venous distention, dyspnea, upperextremity edema

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
check & secure airway: may difficult from upper airway edema; prepare for difficult airway
Elevate head of bed to 30-45°: ↓ venous pressure & facial edema
Supplemental O2 as needed: monitor for respiratory decompensation
Emergent CT chest with IV contrast (via lower extremity IV) to define Obst.
Get tissue dx if not previously established: do not delay tx for biopsy if critically ill

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Known malignancy: lung cancer, lymphoma, mediastinal tumors most common
Central venous catheters, ports, pacemaker/defibrillator leads
Symptom onset & progression: gradual (weeks) vs acute (days)
Dyspnea, facial/neck swelling worse when leaning forward or lying flat
Headache, visual changes, confusion (signs of cerebral edema)
Dysphagia, hoarseness, stridor
Prior radiation to chest
Anticoagulation status

sections.title: Exam
items: Facial plethora & edema: classic finding, worse in morning
Neck & upper extremity venous distension: nonpulsatile
Upper extremity & h& edema (b/l)
Pemberton sign: facial flushing/venous distension when arms raised above head
Chest wall collateral veins (dilated superficial veins)
Stridor or respiratory distress: suggests airway compromise
Mentation changes: suggests cerebral edema
Papilledema on fundoscopic exam

pairs.value: Obst. of blood flow through superior vena cava causing facial/upper extremity edema, dyspnea, & venous distension
Malignancy (60-85%): lung cancer (most common), lymphoma, mediastinal tumors. Thrombosis (10-40%): central lines, pacemaker leads
External compression, intraluminal thrombus, or direct tumor invasion of SVC
Airway compromise & cerebral edema are life-threatening: manage airway FIRST
Most common malignant cause (50%+), esp rightsided tumors
Second most common malignancy causing SVC syndrome
Mediastinal masses in younger pts
Increasing incidence with central lines, ports, device leads
Acute facial/lip/tongue swelling: check for ACEinhibitor use, C4 level
JVD & dyspnea, but with pulsus paradoxus & diffuse edema
Chronic venous congestion, pericardial calcification

sections.title: Management
items: Keep HOB up, give O2 PRN, & use LE IV access when able
Call IR early for SVC stent if severe sx or airway/CNS compromise
Call onc/RT for tumordirected tx; if thrombus is present, start AC if safe
If stridor, cerebral edema, or HD instability: ICU + urgent airway / definitive intervention
SVC stenting (interventional radiology): Fastest sx relief —within hours, >90% success rate
Radiation therapy: for radiosensitive tumors (lymphoma, small cell lung cancer)
Chemothetherapy: for chemosensitive tumors (lymphoma, germ cell, small cell)
Anticoagulation: continue for thrombusrelated SVC syndrome; duration depends on etiology
Monitor for cerebral edema: neurological checks q4h
Maintain head of bed elevation
Continue all meds & fluids via lower extremity access
Treat underlying malignancy per oncology

pairs.value: Via lower extremity IV: defines level/extent of Obst. & guides stenting
May be added to define thrombus extent
Baseline labs; LDH may suggest lymphoma
If thrombosis suspected
Essential for undiagnosed malignancy: coordinate with interventional radiology or surgery
Mediastinal widening, pleural effusion: but CT is definitive

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.notes: Most effective for lymphoma & thymoma. Questionable benefit for or solid tumors: may delay tissue dx.

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.notes: May provide temporary sx relief. Questionable efficacy: use cautiously as pts may already be volumedepleted.

drugs.name: Heparin (UFH)
drugs.notes: If thrombus identified on CT. Goal aPTT 60-80 seconds.

drugs.name: Enoxaparin
drugs.notes: Alternative to UFH for SVC thrombosis if hemodynamically stable.

topics.title: Tumor Lysis Syndrome
topics.subtitle: AKI, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, high uric acid

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
Monitor electrolytes (K, Ca, PO4, uric acid) q4-6h
cardiac telemetry: ↑K causes fatal arrhythmias
Treat ↑K emergently if K >6 or ECG changes (see ↑K topic)

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Cancer type & tumor burden: Burkitt, ALL, AML (high WBC), bulky NHL highest risk
Recent chemotherapy initiation (12-72h prior), including targeted therapies & immunotherapies
Spontaneous TLS possible in highburden tumors without tx
Baseline GFR: pre-existing CKD ↑ risk dramatically
meds: allopurinol prophylaxis? NSAIDs? ACEinhibitors?
Volume status & recent UOP
G6PD status: IDEALLY check before giving rasburicase
Symptoms: nausea, vomiting, muscle cramps, tetany, seizures, palpitations

sections.title: Exam
items: Volume status: JVD, lung crackles (overload), or dry mucous membranes (dehydration)
Cardiac: irregular rhythm, tachycardia (↑K)
Neuromuscular: Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign (hypocalcemia), muscle cramps, weakness
Neurologic: AMS, seizures (severe hypocalcemia or uremia)
Abd: flank pain (uric acid nephropathy), ↓ UOP
Skin: petechiae, bruising (DIC in severe cases)

pairs.value: rapid release of intracellular contents (K, PO4, uric acid, nucleic acids) from tumor cell death
CairoBishop criteria: ≥2 of: uric acid ≥8, K ≥6, PO4 ≥4.5, Ca ≤7 (or 25% change from baseline)
Laboratory TLS + renal failure, cardiac arrhythmia, seizure, or death
Burkitt lymphoma, ALL, AML with high WBC, bulky NHL, CLL with alemtuzumab
Typically 12-72h after initiation of chemotherapy: can occur spontaneously in hightumorburden malignancies
Most common: 12-72h after starting tx for hematologic malignancies
Hightumorburden malignancies without tx; Burkitt lymphoma, ALL with high WBC
Venetoclax, obinutuzumab, lenalidomide: risk may underappreciated
Similar electrolyte pattern (hyperK, hyperPO4, hyperuricemia): check CK
Contrast nephropathy, Obst., sepsis: does not have classic electrolyte pattern
↑K, ↓ BP: but with hyponatremia (not seen in TLS)

sections.title: Management
items: Start aggressive NS: ~200-250 mL/h, goal UOP ≥2 mL/kg/h; strict I&O, Foley if needed
Give rasburicase for high risk or established TLS; avoid K/phos in IVF & diet
Check/treat lytes serially: Ca for ECG changes, insulin/D50 for ↑K, phosphate binders PRN
Call nephrology early for rising Cr, oliguria, refractory lyte issues, or for RRT
aggressive IVF: recheck volume status frequently
Repeat electrolytes q4-6h until stable & trending toward nl. for 24h
Rasburicase: recheck uric acid at 4h: repeat dose if still elevated (on ice!)

Emergent dialysis indications: K >6 refractory to medical management, Cr >10, uric acid >10 with oliguria, PO4 >10, symptomatic volume overload, consulting Nephrology service, esp if calciumphosphorus product continues to rise > 60 mg2/dL
Avoid calcium supplementation unless symptomatic: calciumphosphate precipitation causes renal damage
Hold chemotherapy until electrolytes & renal function stabilize
Transition to allopurinol prophylaxis once acute episode resolves
Restart chemotherapy with lower intensity once TLS resolved (discuss with oncology)

pairs.value: K, Ca, PO4, BUN/Cr: critical electrolytes to trend
≥8 mg/dL meets CairoBishop criteria. Send on ice if rasburicase given
Markedly elevated: reflects tumor cell death. Useful for trending
↑K changes: peaked T waves, widened QRS, sine wave. Prolonged QT from hypocalcemia
Check BEFORE rasburicase: causes fatal hemolysis in G6PDdeficient pts
Required for all TLS pts: fatal arrhythmias from ↑K
Target UOP ≥2 mL/kg/h

drugs.name: Rasburicase (Elitek)
drugs.notes: Recombinant urate oxidase —converts uric acid to allantoin. Must send uric acid on ice (enzyme continues working in tube at room temp, giving falsely low results)Repeat single dose of rasburicase for uric acid rise to ≥ 7.5 mg/dL.

drugs.name: Allopurinol
drugs.notes: Prevention/mild TLS: blocks xanthine oxidase to prevent uric acid formation. Does NOT lower existing uric acid. Start 24-48h before chemo.

drugs.name: nl. saline
drugs.notes: Cornerstone of TLS management. Target UOP ≥3L/24h. Promotes renal excretion of uric acid, K, & PO4.

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate
drugs.notes: Only for symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures, QT prolongation). Avoid routine supplementation: may precipitate calciumphosphate crystals in kidneys.

drugs.name: Sevelamer
drugs.notes: Phosphate binder for hyperphosphatemia. Use with aggressive hydration.

topics.title: Hyperviscosity Syndrome
topics.subtitle: Headache, vision changes, bleeding, AMS, mucosal congestion

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
Emergent plasmapheresis: definitive tx for immunoglobulinmed. hyperviscosity
Protect airway if AMS
Avoid packed RBC transfusion until viscosity lowered: ↑ viscosity & can precipitate crisis

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Known hematologic malignancy: Waldenström, myeloma, polycymia vera, leukemia
CNS sx: headache, confusion, dizziness, strokelike sx, coma
Visual changes: blurred vision, diplopia, visual loss
Bleeding: mucosal (epistaxis, gingival), GI, skin
Constitutional sx: fatigue, weight loss, night sweats
Known paraprotein type & level (IgM MCC)
Prior plasmapheresis txs

sections.title: Exam
items: Neurologic: AMS, focal deficits, nystagmus, ataxia
Fundoscopic: sausagelink retinal veins (pathognomonic), flame hemorrhages, papilledema
Mucosal bleeding: epistaxis, gingival bleeding, oral mucosal petechiae
Skin: purpura, ecchymoses
Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly (underlying hematologic malignancy)
Heart failure signs: highoutput failure from ↑ blood viscosity
Raynaud phenomenon, livedo reticularis (cryoglobulinemia)

pairs.value: Symptomatic ↑ in blood viscosity causing impaired microcirculatory blood flow: hematologic emergency
CNS disturbances + bleeding + visual changes
Most common: Waldenström macroglobulinemia (IgM paraprotein). Also: multiple myeloma (IgA > IgG), polycymia vera, leukostasis (AML/CML blast crisis)
Symptomsoccur when serum viscosity >4-5 cP (nl. 1.4-1.8 cP)
IgM paraprotein: MCC of symptomatic hyperviscosity (10-30% of WM pts)
IgA > IgG3 > IgG1: polymerizes & ↑ viscosity. Less common than WM
Elevated hematocrit causes hyperviscosity: phlebotomy is tx
WBC >100k (AML, CML blast crisis): sludging in microcirculation, esp lungs & brain
Similar neurologic presentation: check serum viscosity & protein electrophoresis
Bleeding + neurologic changes: but low fibrinogen, elevated Ddimer
MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neuro changes: check schistocytes, ADAMTS13

sections.title: Management
items: Start IV NS & avoid diuresis unless the pt is volume overloaded
Definitive tx depends on cause: plasmapheresis for paraproteinemia, leukapheresis for leukostasis, phlebotomy for PV
Call heme/onc STAT for urgent apheresis / cytoreduction planning
Avoid antiplatelets; treat bleeding supportively, including plt transfusion if clinically needed
Plasmapheresis:daily until sx resolve & viscosity returns to normal
Definitive tx: chemotherapy for underlying malignancy (rituximab, BTK inhibitors for WM; bortezomib based for myeloma)
Avoid rituximab initially in WM: causes IgM flare & worsen hyperviscosity
Continue IV hydration between plasmapheresis sessions
Monitor viscosity daily (or surrogate: total protein/IgM level)
Serial neurologic & fundoscopic exams
DVT prophylaxis once bleeding controlled

pairs.value: nl. 1.4-1.8 cP. Symptomatic >4-5 cP. >6 cP = emergency
Identifies paraprotein type & amount
WBC >100k suggests leukostasis; elevated Hct suggests polycymia
PT/INR may elevated from paraprotein interference
Spurious hypoxemia from paraprotein interference: check ABG if SpO2 discordant with clinical status
check renal function & tumor burden
r/o ICH if focal neurologic deficits

drugs.name: nl. saline
drugs.notes: Temporizing measure until plasmapheresis available. ↓ viscosity by dilution.

drugs.name: Hydroxyurea
drugs.notes: For leukostasis —↓ WBC count. Used as bridge to definitive chemotherapy.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.notes: May be part of initial myeloma/Waldenström tx. Discuss with hematology.

topics.title: Cytokine Release Syndrome
topics.subtitle: Fever, hypotension, hypoxemia, capillary leak after immunothetherapy

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
Grade 1 (fever only): supportive care, acetaminophen, monitor closely
Grade 2 (↓ BP /hypoxia): IV fluid bolus, tocilizumab 8mg/kg IV (max 800mg), consider ICU transfer
Monitor for ICANS (immune effector cell associated neurotoxicity syndrome): altered consciousness, aphasia, seizures

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Type & date of immunothetherapy: CART (which product: axicel, tisacel, lisocel, etc.), bispecific antibody, checkpoint inhibitor
Day postinfusion: CART CRSday 1-14
Tumor burden: higher burden = higher risk & severity of CRS
Baseline organ function: cardiac, hepatic, renal
Prior CRS episodes & txs used
Contact information for treating oncology/CART team
Institutional CRS management protocol (varies by center)
Concurrent infections or neutropenia

sections.title: Exam
items: Fever: hallmark of CRS,high (>38.0°C required for dx)
Hemodynamics: ↓ BP, tachycardia: may require vasopressors
Respiratory: tachypnea, hypoxia, crackles (capillary leak: pulmonary edema)
Neurologic ( screen for ICANS): orientation, naming, writing, attention: use ICE (Immune Effector CellAssociated Encephalopathy) scoring tool
Skin: rash, capillary leak with peripheral edema
check for coagulopathy: petechiae, bleeding (DIC common in severe CRS)
Hepatomegaly, jaundice (hepatic involvement in severe cases)

pairs.value: Systemic inflammatory response from massive cytokine release following immunothetherapy: particularly CART cell therapy & bispecific antibodies
Activated immune effector cells release IL6, IFNγ, TNFα: systemic inflammation mimicking sepsis
CART:1-14 days after infusion (median day 2-3). Bispecific antibodies: within 24-72h of first dose
Grade 1: fever only | Grade 2: ↓ BP responsive to fluids, O2 <40% | Grade 3: vasopressors required, O2 ≥40% | Grade 4: multiple vasopressors, ICUlevel support
Most common & severe cause: all commercial CART products carry CRS risk
Blinatumomab, teclistamab, mosunetuzumab: CRSmilder than CART
Rare CRS; more common to cause immunerelated adverse events (irAEs)
Clinically identical: always treat empirically for both until cultures negative
Can occur with or independently of CRS: neurologic sx predominate
Massive ferritin elevation, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly: CRS can trigger secondary HLH
Fever, organ dysfunction: imaging may needed to differentiate

sections.title: Management
items: r/o sepsis: send BCxs/labs & start empiric broad spectrum abx
Grade severity & call the CART / oncology team now
Grade 1: supportive care; Grade 2+: tocilizumab; add dex if worsening or higher grade
Grade 3-4: ICU, pressors/O2 support, tocilizumab + dex 10mg IV q6h
Trend CRP q6-12h: best objective marker of CRS trajectory
Recheck CRS grade q4-6h: escalate tx if worsening
Continue antibiotics until cultures negative at 48-72h & clinical improvement
Tocilizumab: can repeat x1 in 8h if inadequate response (max 3 doses/24h, 4 doses total)
If refractory to tocilizumab + steroids: consider siltuximab (antiIL6), anakinra, or ruxolitinib
Monitor for delayed ICANS (can present days after CRS resolves)
Corticosteroid taper over 3-7 days once CRS controlled
Coordinate closely with CART/oncology team throughout

pairs.value: Best realtime marker of CRS activity: correlates with severity, dropsafter tocilizumab
Markedly elevated in severe CRS (>10,000 suggests HLH overlap)
Elevated but rises paradoxically after tocilizumab (blocked receptor, unbound IL6 accumulates) —don't use to judge tx response
Mandatory: cannot distinguish CRS from sepsis clinically
check cytopenias, organ function, DIC
Fibrinogen, Ddimer, PT/INR: DIC common in Grade 34 CRS
Cardiac arrhythmias in severe CRS
standardized ICANS grading: orientation, naming, writing, attention, commands

drugs.name: Tocilizumab (Actemra)
drugs.contraindications: Active severe infections (relative: still give if CRS suspected)
drugs.notes: Firstline for ≥Grade 2 CRS. IL6 receptor antagonist. Max 3 doses in 24h. CRP will dropafter: useful marker.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.notes: Add to tocilizumab for Grade 34 CRS or refractory Grade 2. May impair CART cell efficacy: discuss with oncology before starting.

drugs.name: Methylprednisolone
drugs.notes: Alternative corticosteroid. Highdose (1g IV daily) for Grade 4 or steroidrefractory CRS.

drugs.name: Anakinra
drugs.notes: IL1 receptor antagonist: for tocilizumab/steroidrefractory CRS. Also effective for ICANS.

drugs.name: Broadspectrum antibiotics
drugs.notes: Give empirically: CRS is indistinguishable from sepsis. Typical: vancomycin + piperacillintazobactam or meropenem.

topics.title: Differentiation Syndrome
topics.subtitle: Fever, edema, pulmonary infiltrates, hypotension during ATRA or arsenic

sections.title: Acute Management
items: Airway: check patency and protect. Breathing: check WOB, oxygenation, and ventilation. Circulation: check pulse, BP, perfusion, and IV access.
Start dexamethasone 10mg IV q12h now upon clinical suspicion: do NOT wait for confirmatory testing
Do NOT stop ATRA/ATO for mildmoderate DS: continue differentiation therapy while treating DS
For severe DS (respiratory distress requiring vent, renal failure, ICUlevel care): temporarily hold ATRA/ATO until resolution,thenrestart at lower dose
Aggressive supportive care: supplemental O2, diuresis for volume overload, vasopressors if needed
Monitor for DIC: common in APL at baseline & may worsen

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Confirmed APL (acute promyelocytic leukemia): must be on ATRA &/or arsenic trioxide
Day of ATRA/ATO therapy: DS 2-47 days after start (median day 7-12)
Initial WBC count: WBC >10k at presentation is major risk factor for DS
Rising WBC during tx: leukocytosis during ATRA suggests differentiation (& DS risk)
Weight gain: key early sign (>5kg suggests significant capillary leak)
Fever: lowgrade, persistent
Dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain
DIC status at baseline (nearly all APL pts have some DIC)

sections.title: Exam
items: Respiratory: dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxia: pulmonary infiltrates & pleural effusions
Volume status: peripheral edema, weight gain >5kg, JVD, crackles
Fever: lowgrade, persistent (but can highgrade)
Cardiac: pericardial effusion (check for distant heart sounds, tachycardia)
Musculoskeletal: diffuse bone pain
Renal: ↓ UOP, rising creatinine
Skin: look for DICrelated petechiae/purpura (common in APL)
Neurologic: headache, AMS (rare but serious)

pairs.value: Lifethreatening complication of differentiation therapy in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL): caused by ATRA (alltrans retinoic acid) or arsenic trioxide
Rapid differentiation of malignant promyelocytes: cytokine release, capillary leak, & tissue infiltration by differentiating cells
~25% of APL pts on ATRA/ATO; can occur 2-47 days after starting therapy (median 7-12 days)
5-10% overall; up to 40% if mechanical ventilation required: early recognition is critical
Retinoic acid syndrome (RAS): renamed b/c arsenic trioxide causes identical syndrome
MCC: used in induction therapy for APL
Same syndrome: occurs with ATO alone or in combination with ATRA
Ivosidenib, enasidenib for IDHmutant AML: similar mechanism, emerging recognition
Most important DDx: APL pts are immunocompromised. BCxs, empiric antibiotics mandatory
DIC in APL: alveolar hemorrhage. CT chest may differentiate
WBC >100k with pulmonary/CNS sx: different mechanism, treated with leukapheresis
From aggressive transfusion support in APL: no fever, no weight gain trajectory

sections.title: Management
items: Start dexamethasone now & hold ATRA/arsenic only if severe
Give O2, cautious diuresis if overloaded, & Foley/strict I&O if needed
Call heme/onc now; restart differentiating tx once sx improve
Do NOT use leukapheresis: this is not leukostasis
Continue dexamethasone 10mg IV q12h until complete sx resolution (minimum 3 days)
Taper dexamethasone slowly over 1-2 weeks: premature discontinuation causes relapse
For mildmoderate DS: continue ATRA/ATO throughout tx with dexamethasone
For severe DS: hold ATRA/ATO until resolution,thenrestart at ↓ dose (ATRA 25mg/m²: consider 12.5mg/m²)
Aggressive DIC management: cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen <150, platelets for plt <30-50k
Daily weights & strict I&O: diuresis for volume overload
Prophylactic dexamethasone: some protocols start dexa prophylactically with ATRA if WBC >5-10k
DS can recur: monitor for recurrent sx after steroid taper or ATRA restart

pairs.value: Rising WBC during ATRA is risk factor: WBC >10k associated with higher DS incidence
B/l infiltrates, pleural effusions, pericardial effusion
Renal function (AKI from capillary leak), hepatic involvement
DIC monitoring: fibrinogen <100 requires cryoprecipitate
Weight gain >5kg is diagnostic clue: track trend daily
Cannot differentiate DS from infection clinically: cultures mandatory
Elevated in DS; helps track response to tx

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.notes: Cornerstone of tx. Start at first suspicion. Continue until complete resolution of sx (minimum 3 days, 1-2 weeks). Taper slowly.

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.notes: For pulmonary edema & volume overload from capillary leak. Monitor electrolytes closely.

drugs.name: Hydroxyurea
drugs.notes: If WBC >10k during ATRA tx: hyperleukocytosis worsens DS. Some protocols add prophylactically.

pairs.key: ICU / immediate higher level of care if
pairs.value: persistent respiratory distress, high-flow or NIV need, hemodynamic instability, vasopressor need, severe arrhythmia, airway risk, neurologic decline, or a trajectory suggesting pt may crash on the floor.
